patients.summary: Postal service supervisor in Granby with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, mixed hyperlipidemia, past recurrent diverticulitis and hyperzincemia, followed since 2018. He quietly stopped his statin in early 2023 and restarted after cardiology; last seen September 2024, then perforated diverticulitis needing sigmoid colectomy in October 2025, known to the practice only from records.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
52 y/o man transferring care. Works as a supervisor at the post office, on his feet a fair amount.

PMH (per pt, prior records requested):
- HTN, on lisinopril 20 for years, no side effects
- Type 2 DM, on metformin 1000 BID, tolerates it, does not check sugars often
- Mixed hyperlipidemia on atorvastatin 40
- Diverticulitis x2, both treated at home with oral antibiotics, most recent 2017. Had a colonoscopy after the second bout, told he has diverticulosis and no polyps.
- Told by his last doctor that his zinc level runs high. No symptoms he knows of. Never treated or worked up further as far as he knows.

PSH: none. No abdominal surgery.
Meds: lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID.
Allergies: none to meds.
FHx: father had a heart attack at 58. Mother has type 2 diabetes. Brother with hypertension.
Social: former cigarette smoker, stopped in 2016. Drinks socially, a few times a month. No drugs. Lives in Granby.

ROS: no chest pain, dyspnea, abdominal pain, change in stools, polyuria, vision change.

Exam: well appearing. BP as recorded. HEENT unremarkable. Neck supple, no thyromegaly. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no masses. Ext without edema, DP pulses 2+. Feet: skin intact, monofilament sensation normal bilaterally. Skin unremarkable.
PHQ-2 0.

A/P
1. HTN: at goal on lisinopril 20, continue.
2. T2DM: on metformin, A1c today. Eye exam due, given list of local optometrists.
3. Mixed hyperlipidemia: atorvastatin 40, lipids today.
4. Hx recurrent diverticulitis: quiet since 2017. Reviewed warning signs, call with LLQ pain or fever.
5. Hyperzincemia per prior records: will recheck zinc with today's draw.
6. HM: Tdap today. Hep C and HIV screen today. PSA discussed, he would like it checked. Colonoscopy 2017 per pt, will confirm with records. Flu shot when available.
RTC 6 months for diabetes, sooner prn.

documents.title: Annual Physical Exam
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
55 y/o M for annual exam. Brought a list of diet questions.

Main question: over the summer he read several pieces saying a glass of wine a day is good for the heart, so he began having one 5 oz glass of red with dinner every night. Wants to know if he should keep it up, given his dad's MI.

Otherwise well. No chest pain or SOB. No abdominal pain, diverticulitis quiet since 2017. Saw optometry in June, no retinopathy.

Meds: lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg BID. Taking them all.
Allergies: NKDA.
FHx: father MI age 58, mother T2DM, brother HTN.
Social: quit cigarettes 2016. Wine as above, no other alcohol.

Exam: BP 135/85. Well appearing. HEENT, neck normal. Heart regular, no murmurs. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender. No edema. Foot exam: sensation and pulses intact, no skin breakdown. Exam otherwise unremarkable.

Labs 10/8: TC 195, HDL 40, LDL 120, TG 175. Fasting glucose 98. CMP and CBC unremarkable, A1c in range.

Assessment/plan:
1. Alcohol and heart health: talked through what those studies actually show. They compare people who happen to drink a little with people who don't, and the non-drinkers include people who quit for health reasons; moderate drinkers also tend to differ in income, diet and exercise. That makes the apparent benefit hard to trust. I would not start or keep drinking for heart protection. One glass with dinner is within low-risk limits and his call; didn't want him to go above that. Better payoff from diet, walking and his statin.
2. HTN: BP a little above my goal for a diabetic. Continue lisinopril 20, recheck at next visit.
3. Mixed hyperlipidemia: LDL 120 on atorvastatin 40, HDL 40. Diet review, less refined carbs, more fiber. Continue statin. Recheck lipids in spring.
4. T2DM: stable, continue metformin.
5. HM: flu vaccine today. COVID series done in spring. PSA due next year.
Follow up 6 months with fasting labs before.

documents.title: Follow-up: cholesterol, diabetes
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Subjective: Back for the 6 month check on lipids and sugar after his October physical. No complaints. Has been doing a lot of reading online about statins and now has two worries: that atorvastatin will damage his liver, and that statins cause diabetes. Says he's half decided to quit it. No muscle aches. Still on lisinopril 20 and metformin 1000 BID. Still 1 glass of wine with dinner.

Objective: BP 132/84. Exam unremarkable: heart RRR, lungs clear, abdomen soft and nontender, no edema.
Labs 4/19: TC 190, LDL 100, HDL 45, TG 150. Fasting glucose 98. Liver panel normal.

Assessment and plan:
Mixed hyperlipidemia with diabetes, HTN and a father with an MI at 58: he is exactly the person a statin helps.
- Liver: serious liver injury from statins is rare; his liver tests are normal after years on it. We'd keep checking.
- Diabetes: statins can nudge glucose up slightly, and he already has diabetes; the heart attack and stroke reduction far outweighs that, and his sugars are well controlled.
- LDL improved to 100 from 120 since fall with his diet changes, which is real progress.
He agrees to stay on atorvastatin 40 for now. Gave him a printed summary to read.
HTN: better today, continue lisinopril.
T2DM: continue metformin.
RTC for physical in the fall.

documents.title: Cardiology consultation
documents.author: cardiology
documents.body:
OUTPATIENT CARDIOLOGY CONSULTATION
Date of service: 04/21/2023
Referring: primary care
Reason: cardiovascular risk stratification

Mr. Coleman is a 57-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and mixed hyperlipidemia who comes after diet and statin counseling with his primary physician. His concern is his own chance of heart disease and what more he can do about it.

He takes his metformin and lisinopril reliably. On direct questioning he admits he quit the atorvastatin about three months ago; he had been uneasy about it since reading about side effects and simply did not refill it after the new year. No muscle symptoms when he was on it.

ROS: Denies chest pain or pressure, dyspnea, or any change in his vision.
PMH: HTN, T2DM, mixed hyperlipidemia, recurrent diverticulitis, hyperzincemia.
PSH: none abdominal.
Medications on our list: lisinopril 20 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily (not taking, see above).
Allergies: NKDA.
Family: father MI at 58; mother type 2 diabetes; brother hypertension.
Social: former smoker, quit about 7 years ago. One glass of red wine with dinner. Supervisor with the postal service.

Examination: unremarkable cardiovascular and general exam.

Laboratory today: hemoglobin A1c 7.2%, fasting glucose 154 mg/dL, total cholesterol 220, HDL 35, LDL 145, triglycerides 200 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, urine albumin/creatinine ratio 250 mg/g.

Impression: High lifetime cardiovascular risk from diabetes, hypertension, atherogenic dyslipidemia and premature paternal coronary disease, with no symptoms to suggest coronary disease today. The jump in LDL from 100 to 145 fits stopping his statin.

Recommendations:
1. Restart atorvastatin 40 mg daily. We spent most of the visit on why; he agreed.
2. Continue lisinopril and metformin.
3. Mediterranean-style diet, 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly.
4. Cardiology follow-up in one year with repeat lipids.

Thank you for this referral.
Outpatient cardiology

CARDIOLOGY CLINIC FOLLOW-UP
Visit date: 04/15/2024

Seen again for ongoing management of cardiovascular risk factors; last here a year ago for risk stratification and his mixed hyperlipidemia. No cardiac symptoms. He reports taking all his medicines, including atorvastatin, every day.

He brought a question: he heard about a clinical trial enrolling high-risk patients that compares a new cholesterol-lowering drug with placebo and counts heart attacks. He wants our opinion on whether to sign up.

Current medications: lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Family history: coronary disease in his father.
Social: nonsmoker, social alcohol.

BP 132/84, HR 78. Examination unremarkable.
Fasting labs: total cholesterol 190, HDL 45, LDL 100, triglycerides 225, glucose 98 mg/dL.

Assessment: Primary prevention in a high-risk patient, LDL back to 100 on atorvastatin.
Trial discussion: explained that he would be randomly assigned to the study drug or a placebo and neither he nor we would know which, that he would stay on his atorvastatin either way, that the drug's benefit and side effects are what the trial is testing, and that participation means extra visits and blood work. Participation is voluntary and he can leave at any time. He has the coordinator's contact information and will think it over. The decision is his.

Plan: continue current regimen; follow up in one year.
Cardiology clinic

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT
Arrival 10/11/2025 18:52

CC: severe abdominal pain, nausea, fever

HPI: 59-year-old man with a history of recurrent diverticulitis, followed by his primary care practice since 2018, with hypertension, type 2 diabetes and hyperlipidemia. Pain started roughly 4 hours ago, shortly after eating. At first it was sharp and severe, then let up for a short time, and is now spread across his whole abdomen and constant. Nauseated, feels feverish. No prior abdominal surgery.

Meds: lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily, metformin 1000 mg twice daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
Social: former smoker, about one glass of wine nightly, postal service supervisor.
Family: father MI at 58, mother type 2 diabetes, brother hypertension.

Triage vitals: T 38.2 C (100.8 F), HR 102, BP 135/85.

Exam: Appears uncomfortable, lying still. Abdomen with tenderness throughout, rebound and voluntary guarding. Bowel sounds diminished.

Results: WBC 16.4 with 88% neutrophils, left shift. Upright chest film shows free air under the diaphragm.

MDM: Peritonitis with pneumoperitoneum; given his history, perforated diverticulitis is most likely. NPO, IV fluids, IV piperacillin-tazobactam, IV analgesia and antiemetic. General surgery consulted at bedside and will take him to the OR tonight.

Diagnosis: perforated diverticulitis with peritonitis.
Disposition: admitted to general surgery.

reports.text: Specimen: sigmoid colon, segmental resection. Gross: segment of sigmoid colon with multiple diverticula and a perforation site with overlying fibrinopurulent exudate. Microscopic: acute and chronic diverticulitis with perforation and acute serositis. Margins viable. Lymph nodes reactive. No dysplasia or malignancy identified.
reports.conclusion: Sigmoid colon: perforated diverticulitis with acute serositis. Negative for dysplasia and malignancy.

documents.title: Operative report
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
OPERATIVE REPORT
Date of surgery: 10/11/2025, case start 23:40
Preoperative diagnosis: perforated viscus, suspected perforated diverticulitis
Postoperative diagnosis: perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis
Procedure: exploratory laparotomy, sigmoid colectomy with primary colorectal anastomosis, abdominal washout
Anesthesia: general endotracheal
Findings: purulent fluid throughout the abdomen from a perforated sigmoid diverticulum. No feculent contamination. Remainder of the colon and small bowel healthy in appearance.
Description: Midline laparotomy. Purulent fluid evacuated. Sigmoid mobilized, resected between staple lines to healthy, well-perfused bowel. Stapled end-to-end colorectal anastomosis, air leak test negative. Abdomen irrigated. Fascia closed, skin loosely approximated.
EBL 150 mL. No complications. To PACU in stable condition.
General surgery

documents.title: Discharge summary
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
DISCHARGE SUMMARY
Admitted 10/11/2025, discharged 10/17/2025
Service: general surgery

Diagnosis: perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis
Procedure: 10/11/2025 exploratory laparotomy, sigmoid colectomy with primary anastomosis (no stoma)

Course: Taken to the OR from the ED the night of arrival. Uneventful recovery. IV piperacillin-tazobactam continued for 4 days after surgery, then stopped. Diet advanced from postoperative day 3, tolerating regular food, bowel function returned. Metformin and lisinopril held while NPO, both resumed before discharge. Blood sugars monitored in house. Pathology: perforated diverticulitis, no dysplasia or cancer. Incision clean and dry at discharge.

Discharge medications:
- lisinopril 20 mg daily (resume)
- atorvastatin 40 mg daily (resume)
- metformin 1000 mg twice daily (resume)
- acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours as needed for pain
- oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed for severe pain, 12 tablets, no refills

Allergies: NKDA
Instructions: no lifting over 10 lb for 6 weeks; call for fever, worsening abdominal pain, wound redness or drainage.
Follow-up: general surgery clinic in 2 weeks; primary care within 1-2 weeks of discharge.

documents.title: Was in the hospital
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Wanted to let you know I was in the hospital last week. My diverticulitis came back bad, they said it busted through and I had emergency surgery that night, they took out part of my colon. No bag thank God. Home since Friday, sore but getting around. Can you get the paperwork from the hospital.

documents.title: RE: Was in the hospital
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: I'm so sorry you went through that, and glad you are home and moving. We'll request the hospital records today. I'd like to see you in the next week or two to look at the incision and go over your diabetes and blood pressure meds; please call the front desk to set that up. Call right away or go back to the ED for fever, worse belly pain, vomiting, or redness or drainage at the incision.

documents.title: Hospital records request
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Request faxed to regional hospital HIM for ED record, op note, pathology and discharge summary, admission 10/11-10/17/25. Pt signed release on file.

documents.title: Hospital records: second request
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Nothing received from hospital. Re-faxed request and called HIM, told 2-3 weeks. Also called pt to schedule post-hospital visit, voicemail left.

documents.title: Your hospital records
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Mr. Coleman, your hospital records finally arrived and I've read through them. The pathology showed inflammation from the diverticulitis and no cancer, which is good news. I still haven't seen you since September of last year and want to check on your recovery, your diabetes and your blood pressure. Please call us to schedule; we have early morning openings.

documents.title: Refill request
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Pharmacy request for lisinopril 20, atorvastatin 40, metformin 1000. Not seen since 9/2024, last labs then. Sent 90 days so he is not without his meds. Needs visit and labs before more refills; message sent.

documents.title: Refill request
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Pharmacy request again for all three maintenance meds. Still no visit. Sent 30-day supply only. Front desk to call and book.

documents.title: Scheduling call
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Reached pt. Says work has been heavy since he went back after surgery and he will call next week to book a physical. Offered 7am slots.

documents.title: Refill request
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Another refill request. No appointment made. Sent 90 days of lisinopril, atorvastatin and metformin to avoid a gap; I'll keep trying to get him in.

documents.title: Overdue physical
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Hello Mr. Coleman, you are overdue for your annual physical and diabetes labs. Please reply or call to schedule. Thank you.
